subject: Chemistry
title: Antimatter: The Mirror of Matter
description: Learn Antimatter: The Mirror of Matter in one minute.

hook.text: For every particle, there's an antiparticle—identical but with opposite charge. When they meet, both annihilate into pure energy.

buildup.text: Paul Dirac predicted antimatter in 1928. Carl Anderson found the positron (anti-electron) in cosmic rays in 1932.

discovery.text: When an electron meets a positron, their combined mass converts entirely to energy: two gamma rays flying apart.

twist.text: PET scans use antimatter. Radioactive tracers emit positrons that annihilate with electrons, producing detectable gamma rays.

climax.text: The Big Bang should have created equal matter and antimatter. Why matter survived is one of physics' biggest mysteries.

punchline.text: Mirror particles that destroy on contact. The universe's most explosive chemistry.

quiz.question: What happens when matter meets antimatter?
options: Both annihilate completely, converting all mass into pure energy
They repel each other like magnets
The antimatter passes through normal matter unchanged

details.summary: Antimatter consists of particles with the same mass as ordinary matter but opposite charge and quantum numbers. When matter meets antimatter, they annihilate each other and convert entirely into energy. Paul Dirac predicted antimatter in 1928, and Carl Anderson discovered the positron in 1932.
details.whyItMatters: Antimatter powers PET medical scanners and challenges physicists to explain why the universe is made almost entirely of matter. It represents the most efficient energy conversion possible.
takeaways: Antimatter has opposite charge but identical mass to normal matter
Matter-antimatter annihilation converts all mass to energy
PET scans detect positron-electron annihilation events in the body

faq.question: Why is there so much more matter than antimatter in the universe?
faq.answer: This asymmetry, called baryogenesis, is one of the biggest unsolved problems in physics. The Big Bang should have produced equal amounts of both, leading to total annihilation. Some slight difference in physical laws must have favored matter, but the exact mechanism remains unknown.

faq.question: Could antimatter be used as a fuel source?
faq.answer: Theoretically, matter-antimatter annihilation is the most energy-dense reaction possible. However, producing and storing antimatter requires far more energy than it releases. Current production methods at facilities like CERN create only nanograms at enormous cost.
